utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. We are continuing with the cross-examination by Ms Residovic. Can we have the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we have the appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honour. I am Giuliano Turone, prosecuting trial attorney. I am here with my colleague Miss Teresa McHenry and Miss Elles van Dusschoten, case manager. Our lead counsel, Mr Grant Niemann, is still out of town. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we have defence appearances? MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honours. I am Edina Residovic, defence counsel for Mr Zejnil Delalic. Together with me in the defence team is Mr Eugene O'Sullivan, Professor from Canada. MR OLUJIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honours. I am Zeljko Olujic, defence counsel for Mr Zdravko Mucic. Together in the team is also Mr Michael Greaves, attorney from UK and Northern Ireland. He is not present this morning at the hearing because he is preparing further evidence materials. MR KARABDIC (in interpretation): My name is Salih Karabdic, defence attorney for Mr Hazim Delic and together with me in the team is Mr Tom Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am John Ackerman, counsel for Mr Esad Landzo. My co-counsel is Miss Cynthia McMurrey. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we continue, please? MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You have not reminded him of his oath, have you? Remind him.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I am reminding you that you are still testifying under oath?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (In interpretation): I understand. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Good morning, Mr Dordic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I would just like to remind you of a part of the discussion we had on Thursday. At that time, Mr Dordic, you said that you worked until 19th April and on 20th April you went to Bradina with your brother, Rajko; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I always -- I continuously lived in Bradina. I worked until 19th and on 20th I came down to Konjic to get my brother Zarko, because he called me on the phone and asked me to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you did not work after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was at that time in administration of the company and Draganic Marko, who was the acting manager, told me that I was going on unpaid leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I was just trying to recall that and bring it up to speed?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. May I remind --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Would counsel kindly give us a breathing space so that it can be interpreted? MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you, your Honours. Mr Dordic, your company was the motel in Konjic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The motel was just one of the units. Otherwise the whole company was called Borasnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Personally -- you personally worked until 19th in this motel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, until the afternoon, after which I went home, because I did not have transportation, so I had to get the bus, if the bus worked. So Tomic Srecko stayed there behind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you. On the south side next to the motel is the house of Mr Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know which side but I know that it's right next to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Next to it and off to the side you can see the entrance to the premises of the discotheque that was on the premises of this house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Over on the other side is where the entrance is up to the apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on the side of the gas station and from there you can see it clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: These business premises worked throughout the period of time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not all the time. Sometimes it would be open; sometimes it would not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: And you could see a number of people, people that you knew, who entered those premises?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While it was working.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Let's go back to the question where we left off when we on Thursday went into recess and stopped the cross-examination. You confirmed that you knew Milovan Gligorevic but you did not remember whether you helped him to get an automatic rifle; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Not translated).

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you know Aleksa Gligorevic, who at that time was in Bradina staying with his grandmother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr Dordic, you also helped him to get a semi-automatic rifle?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: We didn't get a translation to the last question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness nodded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do know Aleksa Gligorevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: But that wasn't what was indicated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I may have said it too soon or something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You wait for the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: And don't nod. Give an oral reply. It has to come on the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Mr Dordic, you knew and you do know Aleksa Gligorevic from Mostar, who at that time was staying with his grandmother in Bradina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do know him, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Hold on. You can go on now. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): You also helped him to acquire a semi-automatic rifle in May of 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what I hear now from you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: What is your answer, whether you did or you did not? What is your answer, not whether you have just heard from counsel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I did not know about this. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): In other words, you did not help him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: On the second day of the fighting in Bradina you said that you, together with a group of 12 persons, decided to leave Bradina because in your estimation the forces attacking Bradina were too numerous; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: And you decided to start going towards the territory that was under the control of the Serbian forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I did not know where we started. We started in the direction across from Mount Bjelasnica so that we would come out at either Hadici, Trnovo or Kalinovik, because we assumed those territories were under the control of Serbs, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr Dordic. As you said, you buried your weapon and you started without a weapon; is that right? You put it away or you had it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: This was done by other persons in your group as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what they did with theirs. I know what I did about my own. I know that none of us had any weapons on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Women and children remained in Bradina because, as you said, you knew that nobody was going to touch women and children; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We assumed that. I regretted having to leave my wife and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr Dordic, you know and later your brother and other people told you about this, you knew that at the same time when you did, another group left Bradina, but in another direction, a group of 30 persons led by your brother, Rajko Dordic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only heard that when I arrived in Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: But you found that out directly then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in Celebici. In Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You also knew that this group was -- you learned that this group also was going in the direction of Kalinovik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Madam, to clarify this, when we got going, we didn't know where the other group was, because this group of 12 that I was in was together.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr Dordic. When you heard from your brother that they also were leaving the territory of Bradina, you learned that they were going in the direction of the Kalinovik municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was only in September of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes, but you learned that directly from your brother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr Dordic, can you tell us, Kalinovik was a stronghold of the JNA before the war, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: And now we all know that this is the birth place of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm just finding this out from you now, that it's the birth place of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr Dordic, you said that you were arrested on Mount Bjelasnica at some very hard to reach place, through which you were passing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: And this place is rather far from Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: This place is not on the territory of the Konjic municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know where it belongs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: If I reminded you, that could be the wider area of the Sarajevo Metropolitan area; that could be either of the municipality of Trnovo or of Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe. I don't know. It could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You didn't recognise anybody among the people who arrested you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You already told us that you knew a lot of people in Konjic as a waiter. The persons who arrested you were not persons from Konjic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe they were. I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr Dordic, you were questioned on Mount Igman and in Tarcin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You don't know who decided that you should be transferred back to Konjic and to Celebici from these places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: As you already stated previously, you found out from your brother that they were taken prisoner near the village of Ljuta. That is also rather far away from Konjic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I found that out after five or six days and Sadik Dzumhur told me this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes, but my question is that the village of Ljuta is fairly far away from Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had never heard of this place Ljuta before. I had heard of another place called Ljuta where there was a fishing pond, but not of this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: This Ljuta that you knew about was near Konjic and this one is in the larger Sarajevo Metropolitan area near Mount Bjelasnica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know, but I have a question. Your Honours, does this have anything to do with this trial, these questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I proceed, your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can proceed. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you. To go back to your participation in the defence of Bradina in the manner that you described before this Trial Chamber, you said you got your rifle from Branislav Gligorevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: And on 25th May 1992 you were occupying a position in Jasika; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Jasika is the hamlet where I was born and where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: That night you spent on the front line with your weapon, from which you did not fire; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What night?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: 25th-26th May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You remained there until the evening of that day, as you stated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Only in the evening you withdrew and you spent the night on the side of a creek?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: And early on the 28th you started towards Mount Bjelasnica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 27th, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: My mistake. I apologise. You said 27th: you stated before this Trial Chamber that in Celebici there existed a commission for questioning of the detained persons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You knew that the President of this commission was Goran Lokas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time I did not know who it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Otherwise you knew that Goran Lokas was the judge in the Demeanors Court in Konjic, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that he worked in the court but I didn't know that he was the President of that court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: In this commission which questioned the detained persons there were also the investigators of the MUP and the representatives of the HVO and the TO of Konjic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know who was there. I know who some individuals were. I know the individual investigators but I don't know who they represented. I was not clear on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because there were investigators who had nothing to do with the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: This commission, Mr Dordic, after your questioning, was putting the detainees into different categories based on what type of weapons these people possessed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What criteria they used, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: But you know that they were putting detainees into certain categories?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We only learned that later. We only found that out later through certain individuals who were there in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: As you stated before the Trial Chamber, since you possessed an automatic weapon, you were placed in the top category?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you confirm, Mr Dordic, that your brother Stravko also had a semi-automatic rifle, which he later turned in and he also acquired through Stravan Vujicic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know who he got it from. I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: But you knew that he had it and that he turned it in, just as you did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You also confirmed that after the visit of the International Red Cross the situation in the Celebici camp improved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only partly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You said that in Hangar 6 there was up to 250 persons and on 31st August 120 of them remained there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We never took count. We never took count there. It was approximately -- that was the approximate number that was told to us by people that delivered food.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: But these are approximate figures, maximum 250 and on 31st August 120 according to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 100-120, between 100 and 120.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: In this period of time between 130 and 150 persons were either released or transferred to Musala; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know where they were going. They were going somewhere. I did not know where they were going, but I know that they were going. On the basis of the knowledge of the guards there, some were going home and some were going to the Sports Hall at Musala.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You also stated that you were in the last group, which consisted of 32 people when in November you were transferred to Musala; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in November; in December.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: There were 32 of you then; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: From August 31st until you were transferred a further 90 men were either released or transferred to Musala; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You also said that your brother, Rajko Dordic, was treated like some kind of a leader or organiser in Celebici; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: He too had an automatic rifle and 150 bullets, which, upon capture, he surrendered. That is what you told you; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never saw him with that rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: But he told you that he had surrendered his weapon when he was captured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have never seen him with a rifle, so please don't try to confuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I apologise if I'm confusing you. I'm just checking some facts which you, as a witness, may be familiar with. Is it true that your position was rather difficult because of your position and relationship with your brother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. Some of the guards would come and torture me psychologically, so that there were moments when I didn't know what to do with myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: In connection with your statements, the statement that you made in the Mraziste Hotel, where allegedly you were questioned by Miroslav Bozic, you said that they treated you correctly. My question is: did you sign that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did, but only it was handwritten. The statement was handwritten.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: The statement you made in Celebici, will you please tell me first -- let us recall who it was who questioned you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Miro Stenek and somebody called Tomic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Were other persons there present while Stenek and Tomic were questioning you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The typist, Ismeta.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What you were saying was dictated and typed on a typewriter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What Tomic or Stenek was saying was typed down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: And they were saying what you had answered in response to their questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably, because I didn't read that statement when I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: But you listened to the dictation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Stenek or Tomic did not mistreat you in any way or apply any kind of force, any threats or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You have already answered my next question, that is that you signed that statement, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: After being transferred to Musala in December, in January in 1993 you were interrogated again; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: At the time the commission included Jasna Dzumhur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that Dino Bektasevic was there. I don't remember the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Dino Bektasevic, whom you knew from before as a judge of the court of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr Bektasevic treated you correctly as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: The statement that you made at the time included what you were saying or consisted of what you were saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You signed this statement too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I should like to ask you, Mr Dordic, with the assistance of the usher, to examine this report and to see whether it is your statement. I have a copy for the prosecution and for the Trial Chamber: can this copy be marked, please, and shown to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can I see this document, please? MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): I did provide a copy for the prosecution. Mr Dordic, do you recognise your signature on this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It shouldn't be like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This is what you said in the court. This is exactly what you said in this court. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember that I signed it like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: It contains all the things that you have just said in this courtroom; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I object, your Honours, or at least know why this piece of paper was not shown to the Prosecution in advance. It was used for impeachment reasons only. If it is a different reason, we should complain, because we didn't have any possibility to see it in advance. Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Is it impeaching him now? Is this impeaching him now? I'm asking counsel: is this impeaching him?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Not in our opinion, your Honour, so I would complain for having not been shown this document in due time to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: It is admitted. It's admitted. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you. Mr Dordic, I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Your Honour, he did not recognise his signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: He said he didn't sign it this way. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I will look at the transcript, what he said. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you, your Honours. I have no further question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Your Honours, we object for the record. He did not recognise his signature, according to what appears in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Did you sign the document? Show it to him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time I only signed "Dordic". I used to sign as "Dordic".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: So you are denying that this is your signature? Are you saying that this is not your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I doubt that it is. I can't claim with certainty, but I doubt that it is. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Mr Dordic, you said that that was the contents of what you said here before this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did say something to this effect, but I doubt what is said about "Mirko". It's written in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Is the surname "Dordic" -- does this correspond to the way you sign it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's similar. It's something like that, but at the time you can find all my documents in Konjic. You can see the way I used to sign my name in those days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: He is disputing his signature. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): A part of his signature. He says that he didn't -- that "Mirko" was not written. So I would like to ask the witness to sign his name several times, since the Trial Chamber cannot admit the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: He has not said anything different from what he has been saying here. Why are you insisting on it? You are wasting too much time on irrelevancies. He has not said anything different from what he has said here. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Very well, your Honours. In that case I withdraw the proposal for the admission of this exhibit. Thank you. I have finished my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Have you any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: We have no questions for re-examination, your Honour. Thank you. Yes, Mr Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have been talking to the Office of the Prosecutor about agreeing to a medical examination for this witness, the last time just before we started this morning, and I am assuming we have such an agreement. If not, then I would make that as a specific request to the court, that he be examined prior to leaving The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: We had actually this agreement and so we agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Very good. Thank you, Mr Turone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think that's the last for this witness. You are discharged, subject to a medical examination before you leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Have you any other witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We do have another witness. He is a protected witness, so there would have to be some sort of rearrangement of the courtroom. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Invite the witness, please. You can swear the witness. Witness M (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask that the witness be seated? Thank you. Sir, am I correct that you have requested that your name and identity not be released to the public or media?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (In interpretation): Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: You will thus be known as Mr M; do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honours, with the usher's assistance, I would like the witness to be shown a piece of paper with his name on it. The defence counsel is aware of his name. Sir, I ask if you can confirm that this is, in fact, your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, your Honour. So the record is clear, the transcript says "N", as in "November". I believe it is "M", as in "Mike".

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Mr Moran is correct. It is "M", as in "Mike". Mr M, how old are you at the present time?

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: What is your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm going to ask, sir, if you can, just to speak up a little bit, to make sure the interpreters can hear you without a problem. Mr M, in 1992 what was your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was working in the Yugoslav railways, marketing of the Yugoslav railways.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Where were you living in the beginning of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a place called Bradina.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were you a member of the SDS at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: In fact, were you an officer within the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you explain what post you held and for what part? Was it the SDS for all Konjic or just for Bradina? Can you just please explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had the post of treasurer in the local committee of Bradina, in the local Bradina committee of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. In 1992, sir, were you armed or were you part of any kind of military or police unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I belonged to the reserve police force for the local board.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were you armed as part of -- being part of this unit, the force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: What kind of weapon did you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you please describe a little bit just about how this unit functions, for instance how many persons there were; did you wear uniforms; was someone in charge; what was the relationship between this police force and the Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the conflict broke out the reserve police force belonged to the municipality of Konjic. Immediately after the outbreak of the conflict people of other ethnic groups -- I'm thinking of the Muslims and the Croats -- they joined other committees, so that there was a shortage of manpower to normally perform their functions on the territory of the local community of Bradina. Upon the call of one of the commanders I accepted and joined as a member of the reserve police force. Before the conflict representatives of various ethnic groups were mixed together evenly. When the conflict broke out, only Serbs remained in Bradina. All the others left.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: So, sir, after the conflict broke out, when you were a member of this unit, was the unit part of the Konjic reserve police or acting more or less on its own, not part of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was acting more independently, because nobody from the Konjic force wanted to come to Bradina.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did the people in this unit, including you, wear uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was someone in charge of your unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the Commander of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you yourself wear a uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were there persons in Bradina involved in patrolling or defending the village who were not part of this -- what you referred to as the police unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Immediately upon the outbreak of the conflict, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did those people wear uniforms and were they part of your unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There weren't enough uniforms, so that everyone didn't have uniform, but they were a part of the defence of the village.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did there come a time when there was military action in Bradina? MR OLUJIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, it is not an objection. Mr Zdravko Mucic asks whether the screen could be opened out a little, because he cannot see the witness from his seat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Da (not translated).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Let him see it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness maybe move closer to the microphone?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Let the witness move closer to the microphone. You can carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Did there come a time when there was military action in Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: When was that approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately May 10th, 11th, 12th.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Later on in May was there also additional military action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After 20th.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you participate in any defence of the village during the military action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were you armed at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: What did you do during the action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me see. We had positions, checkpoints, surrounding the village, on the edges of the village, so that we patrolled and checked movements in the direction of our village.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, let me just maybe ask you more specifically, with respect to the military action that started some time after the 20th, can you just very briefly explain what you did and what happened to you, including whether or not at some point you were captured or arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the attack I was on the southern checkpoint in the direction of the village of Zukici and Sunje, at the checkpoint called Jelovac. The attack began with a generalised shelling and an infantry attack on all the edges, that is along the whole length of the defence lines. The centre of the village where our women and children were was shelled. We tried to set up defences, but people didn't really take it seriously enough and they withdrew. The enemy forces entered the edges of the village. We had to retreat towards the centre. I personally saw the incursion into my native village, where I didn't live later on. I saw with my own eyes the house of my parents burning and all the surrounding houses burning. People who were fleeing reported that more than ten men had been killed in that village, civilian men, that women and children were being expelled, mistreated, beaten, that they were threatening them. I tried to break through to the other part of the locality. However, reports reached us that whoever fled, they were threatening to kill their wives and children, so that I was forced, together with some other married men, to go back to the centre to surrender our weapons and to await our further fate.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: So am I correct, sir, that you surrendered and turned over your weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: The soldiers to whom you surrendered, do you know where they were from, what unit or what force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was night. I didn't see anybody. I could not recognise anyone. I only know that they were members either of the TO or the paramilitary units that attacked our village.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: After you surrendered, sir, where were you brought?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken on a truck and transferred to the Celebici camp.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Just for now can you tell us how long a period of time you spent in the Celebici camp before you were released or transferred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Celebici itself, including the tunnel and the hangar, I spent about three months, a little bit more than three months.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: About how many persons were brought to Celebici at the same time as you as part of the same group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 20 persons as part of the group, but about an hour or two later another 30 persons, maybe even more, were brought into the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Without going into details, sir, can you just simply tell me whether you were or were not mistreated either at the time you were arrested or during the transportation, as you were brought to Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. From the time I was -- from the moment I was captured, I was beaten, and I was beaten during the transportation to the Celebici, and also beaten while taken to the Tunnel Number 9, and throughout my stay in Celebici I was also beaten.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, let me bring you to the time that you first arrived at Celebici. Can up please tell us what happened when you first arrived at the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we were unloaded off the truck in which we arrived at Celebici, we were met by the welcoming committee, as it was called by them, a few strong guys, who took everything we had, and here I mean all the gold, the watches, wallets, keys.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, let me interrupt you just to clarify that. Was anything taken from you personally at this time, anything of value?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. A chain, a ring, wallet. I don't know how much money I had in there. My keys to the apartment. They took all that.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you ever get any of these items back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was there anything of value that you were able to keep?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I managed to hide my engagement ring.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Please continue, sir, with what happened to you after you were brought to Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we were loaded off the truck, those things were taken away from me. We were all beaten. I was beaten personally, and we were put into the Tunnel 9, the so-called Number 9. I saw a few persons there who had been brought in before I did. They were part of my group. We were all beaten up. I bled. My left arm was bleeding and I felt like I was losing consciousness. I asked someone for help and one of them tore their tee-shirt and helped me bandage my arm.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About seven days.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately where you sat within the tunnel? Was it near the entrance, the middle or towards the back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since I got off the truck one of the first, I was sitting in the back of the tunnel, the part where people went to the toilet, around there.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. During the approximately seven days that you stayed in the tunnel were you yourself ever mistreated during that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Would you please tell us exactly what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was brought out by a soldier. I only knew him by sight. I didn't know his name. They made me put my hands behind my head and I was beaten there with some objects and kicked. I fell a few times. I was back up and then again taken to the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did anything particular happen such that the beating of you was stopped or finished?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I think the reason was new persons who had been captured on Mount Bjelasnica were being brought in.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: During the first seven or so days that you were kept in the tunnel were you ever interrogated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Were you ever interrogated at any time while you were in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Would you please just describe briefly your interrogation, when it was and who it was who interrogated you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After about seven days I was transferred to the hangar. I don't know exactly. It was about a month, a month and a half, maybe up to two months in the hangar when I was called out with several other witnesses, and I was escorted to the administration, to the command building, and there we were lined up, our hands against a wall, and we waited to be called in. I was questioned by Mr Mladen Pekar -- sorry -- Kuhar, Kuhar. I knew him personally from the high school and we were colleagues. I was escorted by Mr Delic from the hangar to the command building. I was questioned there. I was insulted. There were different kinds of insults and provocations. I was questioned about the statement and I signed something that I never read. That was on one occasion in Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: After the approximately seven days you spent in the tunnel where were you brought and, if you know, why were you moved from the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately seven days later they told me to pack up and they said to hurry up. We were all beaten up, so we had to help each other to help each other outside. We were lined up against a wall. We supported each other, so that we wouldn't fall. Then we were ordered to turn around. There was a line-up across from us and those were the people that had just been brought in. They had apparently just been arrested. These were our neighbours, our relatives. I think that the reason for us being brought out of Number 9 was to put them in.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Where were you brought, sir, after you were taken out of the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were taken to the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were you ever mistreated, sir, during the time that you spent in the hangar, and I'm not here asking for details? I'm just asking if you were or were not mistreated at any time while you were in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, many times.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: On the occasions when you were mistreated, were you told anything about -- that led you to believe why you in particular had been selected for mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometimes yes; sometimes no.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: On those occasions where something in particular was said to you can you please give us an idea -- could you please give us more details about that? What was said to you that led you to believe why you had been selected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's hard to say why but during one of the beatings Mr Zenga asked me whether I went to church and whether I crossed myself. That was before he started beating me, and I didn't know what to respond. He said: "No", because I didn't have time. I was very busy. Then he started beating me. In other words, the question itself was -- I don't know why this question.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was any mention, sir, ever made about your political activities in Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Not in the sense -- on that sense; more that I was a Cetnik and things like that. I was insulted on ethnic basis.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you please tell us as much as you can chronologically what happened to you when you yourself were mistreated, and if you can, I would like you to tell us the first incident that you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was mistreated and threatened with death, that I would be sentenced to death. I was insulted. "Where are your children and wife?", all these things that really kills you inside, that morally ruins you. You mean -- sorry. I did not understand your question. You mean the first time I was beaten.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: The first time, yes, not the time you were in the tunnel but after you were moved to the hangar, please, the first time that you were beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was beaten up by Kravar. I don't know his first and last name. I know that his nickname was Kravar. I was brought out. I was made to lie down on concrete. They put a wooden stick which was about half a metre long -- it was put into my mouth. I had to keep my hands on the back of my head, and he and another guy, he beat me with the stick and the other one was kicking me. The worst blow came from Kravar in the part of the leg from my knees down to my soles, and then I was also getting blows in the kidney area. That was the first beating after Number 9.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you please tell us the second beating that you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second beating I think was around the time of the visit of I think it was an Arabic television crew. At that time I was beaten by Mr Delic. I received several blows in the hangar itself and then I was brought outside and beaten while the TV cameras were filming. I don't know how long it went on. I know that I received a lot of blows and I was close to losing consciousness. That was the second beating.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Please continue, sir, with the next beating that you remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next beating was -- in my case there was no next beating. In my case it was a daily beating. When I say "beating", I'm referring to being brought out and being beaten up. I do not count in there that Mr Delic would daily come to the place where I was and he would stand in front of me. I had to raise my head and allow him to kick me in my chest area every day. In other words, it was daily. The next beating -- I mean mass beating -- mass beating happened when Messrs -- in fact, Mr Delic brought me out personally, as well as Zenga. They were looking for someone who was working with the railroads. Everybody who did that had to get up, those who worked for the railroads. There were maybe ten, fifteen persons there. Delic took one of them out. The rest of us sat down. Several minutes later this guy was brought back and Delic pointed his finger at me and told me to come out. He brought me to the corner of the hangar. I could hear very well when somebody said: "That's the one".

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, when you say the corner of the hangar, do you mean inside the hangar or outside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Outside the hangar. He took me outside.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: What happened after you heard a person say: "That's the one"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then Delic turned around. He went back about 10 metres from where I was. His car was parked there. He sat into the car. Zenga stayed with me and there was another civilian there. I think he worked for a butcher and he used to keep -- he used to tend to the sheep within the perimeter. On Zenga's order I had to kneel down, put my hands behind my back -- behind my head, the back of my head, and allow him to hit me with karate chops and kick me in the chest area. This went on for a while. He would kick me until I would fall and then he would raise me again and on and on. This went on until I lost consciousness. After that they poured water on me. I came to. He put several pieces of newspaper, made fire, took out a knife.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Who is "he"? When you say "he took out a newspaper and made a fire", who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm referring to Zenga. He heated a knife on this flame and he forced me to take this knife with my bare palm. I took it gingerly and I tried to simulate. However, he took my palms and took them in his own hands so that I could feel my own burnt flesh. He carved a cross into my palm.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say: "He carved a cross"? Do you mean from the burning knife a cross was made on your hand? I'm trying to ask whether or not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Two strokes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm just trying to -- the cross was made from the burns rather than from you being cut with the knife; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. No. No. No. Yes. The cross was burnt in.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that I was brought back into the hangar. I was carried in, because I was not able to come in on my own. My hand was -- looked so bad and hurt so much that I had a swelling and I got an infection of the hand. Several days later after this incident when I was called out by a couple of soldiers to be beaten again, because they told me --

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to actually -- before we move on, I want to ask you: during the time that Zenga was kicking you and held the knife over you, do you remember anything about what was being said? In other words, was anything being said to you or yelled at you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He just told this man who was holding a rifle: "If he moves, shoot".

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: During this incident, including to the time you were brought back to the hangar, did you ever see Mr Delic again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. While I was being beaten, I saw Delic in the Fica, the small Fiat. While I was still conscious he was there all the time. I am not sure he stayed to the end, but he was there for the first five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: About how far away was the car from where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Roughly up to 10 metres, not further.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: At any point immediately after this or at some subsequent point did Mr Delic say anything to you about what had happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When he saw my hand, he said: "If anyone asks, you know what happened. You were smoking, you fell asleep and that's how it happened".

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you remember when it was that Mr Delic told you this, to tell someone that you'd fallen asleep with a cigarette?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Inside the hangar, when I was thrown in. When I reached my place he came up to me and said. "Do you know what you were doing? You were smoking and you fell asleep".

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Going forward now, sir, you were starting to tell about a couple of days later when you were called out of the hangar again. Can you please describe what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a few days later, maybe two or three days later, I was taken out by two soldiers. I think they were not guards. They told me that I had greetings from a neighbour in Repovci and that they would hand it to me in person, these greetings. I was taken out and in spite of the condition I was in, one of them said: "Look, I can't beat him in this state. Take him back". So I was taken back without being beaten on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you describe after this what kind of -- in the period after you had been kicked and burned what kind of visible injuries you had, if any?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The injuries were obvious on my palm. My palm was totally swollen. There were no visible injuries on the skin, but I was beaten up. I couldn't stand. I couldn't move. I was unable. You couldn't see anything on my face, but at first glance you could see that I had been beaten up. That's why I was released.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: What happened to your hand? Did it heal immediately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. For a long time it was very painful. My palm was like this (indicating), so big. It was like a large apple. There was pus underneath, I don't know what. After the blister burst and when it started to fester, only then was I allowed to be seen by a doctor. I received -- I don't know -- an ointment and this helped me.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Who gave you the ointment, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr Relja, the doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was there any other time, sir, other than what you've already told us, about where you were mistreated in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The next beating occurred I can't remember exactly how many days later, but I was taken out at night. I was taken out. Before me Lazar Savic had been taken out and beaten up. Then it was my turn. I was taken out. Zenga and Delic were waiting for me outside with three other men, who were not from Celebici, who were from Tarcin, called Repa, Gumeni and Paja. I had to lean up against the wall. Somebody put a mask on my head from behind, a gas mask. The mask was tightly screwed on. I couldn't breathe. I was ordered to lie down on the concrete. They took off my trousers as far as the knees. Then I felt that they put some powder over me. I couldn't feel pain. I could just feel something dropping on me. I was taken by hands and legs and placed under the manhole. Then I was showered with water. Then I felt terrible pain and terrible burns. After that came the beating, all over my back from my back to my legs. I felt the worst pain in the lower part of my back, the pelvic bone. At first the worst thing was the lack of air. I was choking. I tried to remove the mask and I couldn't. Maybe after some time -- I don't know how long it was -- but I know that I lost consciousness several times. The last time I came to I felt air that I could breathe. The mask had been removed. Only then did I feel the terrible pain in my back and in the area of the pelvic bone. They forced me to go into the hangar. I tried to move as soon as possible fearing fresh blows.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Who told you to go back to the hangar, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of them. I can't remember who it was. I wasn't quite all there. I tried to reach the hangar as quickly as I could, but I couldn't move. Then they threw me into the hangar, two of them. They just threw me inside the door. Then I asked one of the prisoners to help me reach my place. Nobody dared. After a few minutes my brother approached and he literally dragged me to my place, and Delic came in then and took my brother out. He received a couple of blows for helping me to reach my place. He didn't stay out long.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you have any injuries? Were you injured at all as a result of this beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Injuries? Again they were not visible. It was not my skin that had been injured. I had five ribs fractured. I had my pelvic bone fractured. I was immobile for 12 days. My father helped me. I even couldn't use the toilet. I couldn't go outside. I had to do it on the spot. My father moved my arm, my leg, my body. He would place me in a position that suited me better.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, when you talk about bones being broken, is this something you were told at the time, or were you told this afterwards? I mean, was it something you were told while you were at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Nobody examined me at all. I had no medical treatment.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, going back, for this incident that you just described, do you remember exactly who it was who called you out for this beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For this last incident?

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Delic, Delic.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Then after you were outside, before the gas mask was put on you, who were you able to observe outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Delic, Zenga and three men from Tarcin, as I said, Gumeni, Pava and Repa -- Paja.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: As soon as the gas mask was put on you, were you able to tell or see who was doing the beating or other things you have described with the powder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I couldn't see. It was night, the gas mask was on my head. I was fighting for my breath. I couldn't even think or look or anything.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, was that the last time you were mistreated that you remember? Severe mistreating. I know you have already discussed some daily activities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So severely, yes. In addition to the daily events, the visit of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me -- sir, you mentioned Zenga. Can you tell us, if you know, what Zenga's real name is and if you knew him from before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He was younger than me. I didn't know him before the war. I heard from the prisoners that that was his name and they all called him like that. So I didn't know him from before.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: What was Zenga's role in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zenga's role in the camp, you should ask Mr Delic and Mr Pavo, but my personal opinion was that he was the right hand, the executioner, the man who executed their orders. Sometimes he decided independently.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, do you know whether or not Zenga was a guard at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: During the time that you were at the camp, did you ever learn his real name, or did you always just know him as Zenga?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew him as "Zenga". Somebody who knew him from before, who went to school with him, said his name was Osman.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was anyone else called "Zenga" at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I think not.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you hear anything else besides "Osman" for the real name of Zenga?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew his surname as well, but I can't recall it just now.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I later learned in Musala.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What did you learn in Musala, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The name and surname, Osman Landzo, because after a year and a half or two, I think, he was imprisoned as a prisoner in the same prison that I was in in Musala.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you have also mentioned a Mr Delic. Do you know Mr Delic's full name and did you know him from before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hazim Delic, I knew him from before, not in person, but there were many of my friends and relatives who worked with him. I knew him from before the war, not in person, but by sight.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: What was his role in the camp, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During my transfer from Number 9 to the hangar Delic had some problems with his leg. I don't know what kind of problems. I know that he limped, and he sat with the prisoners, the people he knew. I know that he even gave them cigarettes. However, afterwards I think that his role was one of command, of somebody that the guards and prisoners feared, somebody who gives the orders.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: How frequently would you see Zenga in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zenga, I would see him daily, every day during my stay in Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: How about Mr Delic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we can stop here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: And come back at 2.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: We will go for lunch and return at 2.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly remind the witness he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I should like to remind you that you are still testifying under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Mrs McHenry, you can continue. You can carry on with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, right before the lunch break I was asking you how frequently you would see Mr Hazim Delic in the camp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Almost every day. At first not so often, but the last two months, almost every day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He says "every day almost".

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. I was just about to say there was a problem with the interpretation. Sorry. Sir, you also mentioned before Mr Pavo. Can you tell us who you mean by Mr Pavo and what his role was in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pavo Mucic I mean. I knew him as I did Mr Delic, by sight, not personally, but I knew a little more about him, because my brother worked with him. He knew him and was a friend of his. I knew Pavo Mucic by sight and I saw him in the camp. The first time when he was touring the hangar accompanied by Mr Delic and a couple of other guards. So the first time was about 20 or 25 days after my capture.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: What did you understand his role in the camp to be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My personal opinion is that he was somebody who was in charge, who was in command, somebody the guards feared, who gave orders to the guards, somebody the guards were responsible to.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you tell us specifically what you saw or what you were told when you were there about Mr Mucic's role, for instance, before he came into the hangar, would the prisoners be told anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion, on one visit by Mr Mucic to the hangar the guards ordered that we put the hangar in order, that we take our positions, because sometimes people would relax a little, they would stretch their legs out a little. We had to take up our positions properly, because Pavo was coming. Those were the comments of the guards and those were the orders they received.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: During the times that Mr -- did you ever see Mr Mucic and his interaction with the guards when he came into the hangar? Would he say anything to the guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I only saw Pavo inside in the hangar. When he would enter the hangar he was accompanied by Mr Delic and another one or two guards. He would sort of review the prisoners. He would make a circle round the hangar. The people he knew he would talk to. Those he didn't he just passed. He exchanged a few words with my brother. As for me, he just looked at me and passed by and didn't say anything. So that I'm sure that Pavo was somebody who was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: During the times when he would come into the hangar did you ever see Mr Mucic say anything to the guards, direct them in any way? Let me ask you more specifically: where would the other guards be when Mr Mucic was in the hangar and how would they know to be in a particular place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One or two were escorting Mr Mucic and one of them would stand at the door with a weapon as a kind of precautionary measure. There were those that were inside and there was one standing guard at the door.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you ever see Mr Mucic say anything or direct any of the guards about where a guard should or should not be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't see it, see that. This wasn't happening inside; probably outside.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. How frequently did you see Mr Mucic in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During my stay in Celebici not many times. Maybe four or five times, not more.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you ever see any interaction between Mr Mucic and Mr Delic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not a conversation but I could give an example in the case of one prisoner. Pavo approached the prisoner, accompanied by Delic. The prisoner had to get up. They were talking. Pavo wanted the prisoner to be -- no, Delic wanted the prisoner to be released. Pavo was against it. He was saying that he was a Cetnik. Delic seemed to be for his release and Pavo was against his release. So there was obviously disagreement between the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was that prisoner released or not, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time no, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, in addition to the mistreatment that you yourself suffered, did you ever observe any mistreatment that other prisoners suffered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, many prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not while you were at the camp any prisoners died?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Died? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Could you please tell the court what you yourself observed concerning the mistreatment of any prisoners that may have died while in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are thinking of the camp itself, not upon them being brought in? In the camp itself at the very beginning when people were unloaded from the trucks and put into Number 9, all the prisoners were bitten with sticks, rifle butts, boots, whatever they could lay hands on, so that each and every one of them were beaten up really. During my stay in Number 9 many of them were beaten again, not all of them -- MR OLUJIC (in interpretation): Objection, your Honour. The witness was asked whether he saw anyone being killed. He is not responsive to the questions. He is talking about mistreatment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: He can carry on. I think I overrule you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Your objection is overruled. It was mistreatment that he was asked about and that is what he was saying. Go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I understood the question, it was mistreatment and beatings. So the prisoners were beaten in Number 9 itself. When I was transferred to the hangar, I came across many people who had been beaten up, who were immobile, and during my stay in the hangar for about three months I personally experienced and eyewitnessed the beating of many people. I don't know the number. 20 or 30 people. I saw people die from this beating. A number of them died from the consequences of the beatings. All this I witnessed myself.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, could you please tell us about any incidents where you yourself observed mistreatment which resulted in someone's death?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I saw the mistreatment of Bosko Samoukovic, who succumbed to the consequences of the beatings. I saw the mistreatment of Zeljko Cecez, who also died from the beatings. I saw the beating of Mr Pero Mrkajic, who also died from the consequences. I saw the dead body of Avramovic. I don't know when he died. I didn't see him beaten up but I saw his dead body. I saw the bodies of Miso Kuljanin and Zeljko Klimenta, known as Keljo, and many, many other people who did not die from the consequences of beatings, but who were in a terrible state.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let us go through this, sir. I believe the first name you mentioned was Mr Bosko Samoukovic. Could you please tell us what you observed concerning what happened to Mr Samoukovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr Samoukovic was called out. Why I don't know. He was an elderly man. He was in his 50s or 60s. I'm not sure. He was called out, I don't know for what reason, as I said. He was beaten up by Zenga at the entrance to the hangar, just in front of the door, with a wooden plank, a thick one, which was used to prop up the hangar door. He was beaten up on his back, kidneys, head. They didn't make any point about where they would hit him. He was dragged to his place afterwards and he died from the consequences of these beatings. Two sons of his were there, who watched all this.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not -- do you remember whether or not Mr Samoukovic died in the hangar or outside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he died outside. Actually he was in the hangar in an unconscious condition. He wasn't dead but he was near the end. I'm not sure. I couldn't check. I think he was carried out unconscious, half dead. Maybe he did, but I can't tell for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, what, if anything, did you observe about Pero Mrkajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Pero was imprisoned in the hangar before me while I was still in Number 9. When I was transferred to the hangar, I found Pero with visible wounds, injuries on his head, behind his ear, all over his body. He looked terrible. He was bleeding from his mouth. He couldn't move. He couldn't walk. He couldn't eat. He didn't die in the hangar itself. I think he was transferred perhaps too late to the infirmary, and we later learned that he died.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: What, if anything, did you observe concerning Mr Zeljko Cecez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zeljko Cecez, yes, he died in the hangar. He was taken out. One could have heard his cries, his moans, his pleas that they stop. It was terrible to listen. He was letting out animal-like cries. Then he was thrown in like a sandbag. He was dragged to his place. He begged us to help him. Nobody dared. He died in terrible pain. Many people saw this, all the people who were there. They could have seen the terrible pain he died in. He died in the hangar and he was taken out as dead. The guards would usually close the door, if we tried to walk around or move around a little, to exchange a couple of words. So it was quite obvious that he was dead when he was taken out.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: When you say it was quite obvious that he was -- I'm not sure that I understand you. How is it that you can say that it was quite obvious that he was dead? I'm not sure I understood your explanation. If you could just say it again maybe in different words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not a doctor to be able to ascertain somebody's death, but I know what a dead body is, no signs of life, no sound coming from him, nothing. I can't establish as a doctor somebody's death, but I know what a dead body is. After all his suffering, his moans and cries, they all came to a stop and he went cold.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Mico Kuljanin can you please tell us what, if anything, you observed concerning him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mico was taken out, outside. He was beaten up before, but not that time. He was taken out. We heard a shot. People didn't dare go out for a long time. Some people had to go out. I was one of them that had to go to the toilet and we saw a body lying there, a motionless body, the body of Mico Kuljanin, so outside, not in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, Zeljko Klimenta, can you please tell us what you observed concerning him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zeljko Klimenta was one of the prisoners that the guards knew. He may have had friends among them, acquaintances certainly. I don't know if they were friends. Zeljko Klimenta was someone who could smoke. I think it was Pavo himself who brought him some cigarettes, or someone else -- I don't know who -- so he could smoke. He could go out. He communicated with the guards. He talked to them. The day he was killed Garo was outside with him. He was a man who was distributing food. When Garo came in he just said "they've killed Zeljko". We just fell silent and feared who would be the next. The body of Klimenta we could see when we went out to the toilet.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, when you say -- who was it who came in and said: "They've just killed Zeljko"? Could you please just give us that name again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember the name. I know he was called Garo and he distributed food to the prisoners. The prisoners would bring the food in front of the hangar and Garo would distribute the food in the hangar. He was one of the people who contacted with the guards who could go out. So he probably saw, witnessed the killing himself.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: I just want to clarify. It was Garo who came into the hangar and said: "They have just killed Zeljko"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. How long after this was it that you saw Mr Klimenta's body outside? How long after someone came in and said they had killed Zeljko approximately? The same day or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the same day, maybe two or three hours later. I can't remember. Not immediately, because we didn't dare go out. Two or three hours, maybe four hours later.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, do you know who Mr Vaso Dordic is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
