utterances.text: Can you tell us what, if anything, you observed concerning the treatment of Mr Vaso Dordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As we were sort of senior prisoners, maybe he came a month after us, anyway after us, after some time, he was brought in and I think that at that time he was the one who was beaten most, mistreated most, insulted. Everybody somehow focused on him, because apparently he was subsequently arrested. He was a Cetnik. He was in hiding. So he suffered terrible mistreatment and insults. He even had to do something with his brother. He had to do certain things upon orders of certain gentlemen, certain things that I can't even put in words.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, as much as you can, I would ask that you please tell us what exactly you saw, what this person had to do upon the orders of certain gentlemen. Can you please explain, although I know it is uncomfortable, who these gentlemen were and what you saw happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Beating, non-stop beating. He had to do push-ups, beaten up as he was, and while he was doing it, he would usually get a kick in the kidney area. Together with his own brother he had -- I don't know if I -- he had to have oral intercourse on orders of the guards and I cannot remember which guard it was who ordered that, but the fact was that this transpired and there are witnesses. Not everybody in the hangar, but those from whose vantage points it was possible to see, those can testify to this.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, do you know who Mr Zejnil Delalic is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zejnil Delalic I knew also by sight. I sat in his cafe. We knew before the conflict that this gentleman was arming the paramilitary units of the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, can I just ask: did you ever see Mr Delalic in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you just tell me when, on how many occasions, where he was when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only saw him once. We had been taken to unload some trucks inside the Celebici camp behind a hangar. There were several of us. That is the last time I saw Mr Delalic. He was escorted by two -- I think they were bodyguards or something. They had brand new camouflage uniforms. They had modern weapons and they were well-groomed. We were lined up in front of the hangar and I think he was about five to ten metres away from me. He did not come over. He did not pay attention to us. We just saw him from there.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, was there a time in the camp when the Red Cross came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just a minute. What was he unloading?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am sorry. Pardon, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What was he unloading?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, if you remember, what were you unloading from the trucks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Weapons and ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, can you please tell the court what happened after the Red Cross visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. During the visit itself of the ICRC we were registered. We received registration cards. They at first tried to talk to us. However, the guards and the personnel in the camp, they would not leave. They would not leave us alone with them. So they were present there. Then there was a lady who was a representative of the Red Cross. She tried to intervene and she insisted and only after she openly requested them to leave, they left and we were free to talk to them. We knew that maybe we would suffer consequences later, but we had to tell what happened, so we told them what happened. After they left the hangar, we -- because there were three or four guards per group, we all received a lot of beating and then there was more mistreatment and insults. They would say something like: "You'll never live to see another Red Cross again", things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you tell us who it was who was present when you and the other prisoners were beaten after the Red Cross visit? Can you just explain exactly what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Delic was present. He stood at the door. There was a group of three guys, three guards. They entered and they started to the right and the other three started to the left, and prisoners were sitting down as they were usually sitting. They had to get up, turn around, face the wall, turn their backs to the guards, and then we would get kicks and blows with different instruments to the backs, the kidney area. People cried and moaned. I can give you some details. In the row where I was there was a certain Osman Dedic who came up our way and he told us: "Scream" he said and he would simulate blows. He would put the boot on the back and people would scream as if they were receiving blows but Mr Delic saw this and then he made this row receive beatings again, this part of the row. Throughout the time Delic stood at the entrance of the hangar and observed as prisoners were being beaten.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: How long after the Red Cross visit did you stay in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not long, maybe one month.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Where did you go when you left Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was transferred to the Musala camp.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Could you please tell us the circumstances of your transfer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not certain whether this was luck or not. My brother knew certain gentlemen because they worked together in the electrical utility company, and my brother was promised that he would be transferred. He made a request on my behalf, whether I could be moved with him. So that could be a reason or maybe just luck. I don't know, one or the other.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you know who it was who promised your brother that he would be transferred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was Mitke. I am not sure about his last name. I think it was Mitke and I think he was some chief within the police. So the first name would be Mitke. I don't know about the last name.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Musala?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: More than two years. Two years and two months, something like that. I don't know exactly, but over two years certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were criminal charges -- were you ever told that you were being prosecuted and criminal charges were being brought against you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Excuse me for one second, your Honours, please. No further questions for this witness, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We'll proceed in this order. First, counsel for Mr Delalic; second, counsel for Mr Mucic; third, counsel for Mr Delic; and, fourth, counsel for Mr Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can proceed. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, can I proceed? Good afternoon, Mr M.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you may know, I'm Edina Residovic and I am defence counsel for Mr Delalic. Perhaps it is usual for the rest of us, but since you and I are meeting for the first time, I would like to ask of you what the Trial Chamber usually asks me, so that we would talk slowly, that you should wait for the question to be interpreted and then you answer and I will wait for the interpretation. It is the only way that we can be followed by everybody in the courtroom, otherwise you and I would not need these pauses, because we understand each other. So thank you. Mr M, your family is rather large in Bradina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you are related one way or the other with the Mrkajic family; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We are not closely related.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Through your mother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You stated that you worked for the Sarajevo railroad company and probably on that duty you must have often travelled between Sarajevo and Konjic and Konjic-Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that some time in the middle of or more precisely around 20th April the traffic on this stretch stopped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This railroad traffic stopped because of certain events that went on in Sarajevo and also because of some checkpoints that were erected in Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, that was not the reason.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, the railroad traffic had stopped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on the stretch between Jablanica and Mostar. That is where it was first interrupted and much later it was towards Bradina.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In this -- on this stretch certain combat operations between the JNA and the TO and the HVO had already started in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr M, at the same time, as far as you recall, also the road traffic on the highway which was called M17 was also interrupted between Mostar and Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Much later, and there were checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Can you tell me when this was? Around April 20th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At least ten days before the highway traffic was interrupted the railroad traffic was interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So the legal authorities set up control points of the reserve police on that stretch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the centre of Bradina and on the other side of the tunnel there were also checkpoints set up, the ones that you have mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the checkpoints of the legal authorities before the conflict itself. That was the regular police forces, which were reinforced by the reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You are trying to say that the police station of the MUP in Konjic was assigning the policemen who were supposed to man this checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was just before the conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mean before 6th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, Mr M, as a member of the SDS party and as a treasurer in the local board in Bradina, you had a duty to gather money for the defence of Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, you received weapons from the reserve forces of the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I personally got my weapons from the reserve police of the Konjic MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You received this in the period before April 6th, when you were still part of the reserve units of the legal authorities of the Konjic government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I received these weapons after I pulled out of the reserve of the police and after the Muslim and Croat members of the reserve forces did pull out, and then we were invited by the Commander of the reserve forces to fill in those positions.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you tell us what your commander's name was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr Spasoje Mrkajic.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr M, so you, Mr M, received your personal weapons from Spasoje Mrkajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the reserve police forces.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr M, is it true that you were in Mr Zaro Mrkajic's cafe at the time when 50 automatic rifles were brought there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr M, could you please tell me whether it is true that after 6th April, that is after the proclamation of independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, within the SDS an extreme wing was formed, to which you yourself did not belong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An extreme wing? You must explain that to me.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Which insisted on the accelerated arming of the population and on the forming of certain authorities in Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You can name it whatever you would like, extreme or non-extreme. These people lived there and they wanted to protect their own homes and their wives and children and they said that if nothing came out of the negotiations, they wanted to make sure that they would protect their mothers and families. So this was not the extreme wing. They just wanted to make sure that they could protect their homes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr M, that in this council Damjan Dordic, Dragan Vujicic, Desimir Mrkajic were all elected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't know who was elected in it. I don't know how extreme this wing was, but I know that there was a legal body and we looked for ways and we thought we found a way that we would get in touch with neighbours from Zukici, Sunmir and other villages around there, and we managed to talk to them several times.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr M, wouldn't you say that you were fairly politically active at that time and as far as I know the facts, you took part in negotiations that you are referring to three times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr M, do you know that the legal authorities in Konjic asked of you and in fact made an ultimatum that you surrender arms and remove the checkpoints that were in Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The gentleman who actually spoke to the Konjic authorities, Mr Vaso Mrkajic, knew this and he said -- not that they decided. They said that it was an ultimatum, that should we not surrender arms that Bradina will be levelled to the ground. That's exactly how he put it. So people were scared.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr M, up until 25th May and because of the reasons that you mentioned, no weapons were surrendered and no checkpoints were dismantled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Weapons were not surrendered and the checkpoints were not dismantled because there was checkpoints in Zukici below Bradina and because the tunnel had been blown up by the paramilitary formations, not by the legal authorities in Konjic, and on the other side of Bradina, towards Tarcin, the tunnel was also caved in and so there was no communication on the other side. So no legal negotiations were possible. So it was all like that.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr M. Did you know that at that time members of the Serbian people were coming to Bradina from other places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were coming to Bradina because they were scared. They were expelled from other places and they were fleeing to Bradina. That's from Brdjani and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In one of your statements before you said that there were about 600 people in Bradina. Can you tell us whether it is true that since other people arrived in Bradina from surrounding settlements during these combat operations there were about 1500 people in Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the exact number. There were a lot of people from other villages, a lot of women and children and the elderly, because people were fleeing their own homes. There were many more than the locals.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke in some detail about how you defended the village during those combat operations. Is it true what you stated before, that about 300 people attempted to defend Bradina during those days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately, yes. However, not all of them were armed.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true, Mr M, that the mortar in Bradina was located above the butcher's shop of Mica (sic) Delic and two additional mortars were brought in on the eve of the attack on Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know anything about mortars. I don't know that they even existed. I doubt that they even existed.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: During these combat operations in Bradina you said that you were holding your positions. Was that above the railroad station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. That was across from the railroad station at the place called Jelovac.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr M, we already clarified that this -- the events that I'm referring to happened before 6th April. Now following April 6th do you know that in the middle of April -- you may not know the exact date but this was probably -- this was on 17th April that the Assembly in Konjic proclaimed general mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But the truth is that you -- at that time you did not report as an able -- militarily able person either in the municipality or in the police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not dare come to Konjic at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you stated in direct examination and in answer to the Prosecutor's questions, you virtually created Serbian police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. This was a continuity of the police force that had already existed in Bradina before that.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr M, the Vice President of the Assembly in the Konjic municipality was Duro Kuljanin who was a Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You surely know that he left his post and he went to the Borci Lake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I know is that he had been beaten up and then he fled to Borci.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And Borci is to the east of Konjic town on Mount Prenj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In that period Borci were controlled by the JNA and the Serbian forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr M, I only have a few very quick questions based on -- relating to your political activities. Do you know that in early -- in the first part of April the SDS in Konjic adopted a decision that they would not participate in the defence of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. In the defence of Konjic that's not clear at all.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the SDS at that time adopted a decision on the establishment of the Serbian municipality of Konjic which included all settlements outside of the central municipal area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: With respect to your stay in Celebici, Mr M, would you please look at the model that is in front of you? I would like, with the assistance of the usher, if you could show us Hangar Number 9 where you were located?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Before the witness moves, let me just point out that the witness is protected and I'm not sure how he can point to it without leaning over and being seen. So I have no objection if we want to go into private session or maybe if Ms Residovic wants to show him something and ask if that's correct. I wouldn't object to that either. I just note that this is a protected witness. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can come forward.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do not wish to show myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You can come forward so that you can see what you are showing. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Mr M, is this the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is. I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me am I showing correctly if I say that this is Hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you show us?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just ask -- I know there are people in the front row. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): I think it can't be seen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If they can see me, I'd rather not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You can put the shutters down and he can come up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, if that is a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, a modest suggestion. Perchance -- perhaps the TV people could focus on the model, and each one of the buildings has a letter number on top of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The people sitting in the public gallery, he doesn't want to see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: What I was thinking, your Honour, was if the TV people focused on the model, he could sit down and look at the TV monitor, and since each building has a letter on it, he could identify it that way, off the television screen. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honour, I can adjust my questions so that the witness, without exposing himself to any danger can answer them. So my question is: the building I showed, you say, is not Hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please will you tell me do you know that in only one of these hangars, with the exception of Tunnel Number 9, that prisoners were accommodated in Celebici, in only one of these hangars?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know only in one except for Tunnel Number 9 and the infirmary, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the area of the Celebici barracks is enormous, as can be seen from the model, several hectares, several hectares?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Da (not translated).

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I didn't get the translation of the prior question. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Let me repeat my question. The area of the Celebici barracks, is it very large, covering several hectares?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depends what you imply when you say "large". Several hectares, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me: do you know that in a part of this area of the Celebici Barracks there were warehouses of the Territorial Defence for military supplies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know but I do know that I personally unloaded arms, weapons, ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You don't have to lean over.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating) In one of these two hangars I personally unloaded weapons and ammunition together with other prisoners. I was taken from Number 6 and led over there.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me show once again. So here, this is where you unloaded weapons (indicating) once?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not once; several times.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr M, when you were in Hangar Number 6, all of you, including yourself, you were wearing your own clothes, those that you had when you were captured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of your stay you were not given any special clothing; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, we were not.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that you were interrogated by a commission in Celebici. When you were transferred to Musala, were you interrogated again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion you were interrogated by a commission including Mrs Jasna Dzumhur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were treated well during the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not very correct. There were a lot of provocative questions, and when I was taken from Musala to the police building I was provoked by the guards and the escort.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your statement was recorded; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you sign on that occasion what you had said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did sign something that I didn't read. I could not read it.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr M, do you know that later criminal charges were brought against you for the possession of weapons without licence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that you were pardoned and the proceedings suspended in order for the exchange to take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any other cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: MR OLUJIC (in interpretation): May I, your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can proceed. MR OLUJIC (in interpretation): Thank you, your Honours. Good afternoon, Mr M. My name is Zeljko Olujic. I am defence counsel for Mr Zdravko Mucic. I hope you are still capable of answering my questions, because you have been talking all day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like a break, but I can manage.

utterances.speaker: MR OLUJIC
utterances.text: I won't question you long. I will be relatively brief. Mr M, you said that throughout your stay in Celebici you saw Mr Zdravko Mucic only four or five times; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR OLUJIC
utterances.text: The four or five times that you saw him during a long period of your stay there, was anybody ever mistreated in his presence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In his presence? I would have to remember.

utterances.speaker: MR OLUJIC
utterances.text: As far as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mistreated, no, but he personally insulted me.

utterances.speaker: MR OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. You mentioned, Mr M, that a certain Mitke -- I think that's the name you used -- helped you to get out of Celebici and to go to Musala; is that so? Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I know that my brother tried through Mitke. So I said it may have been through Mitke or maybe it was just good luck. My brother did try to intervene with Mitke to have me transferred, but nobody ever told me -- Mitke never told me: "I helped to have you transferred". So it may have been him or some luck.

utterances.speaker: MR OLUJIC
utterances.text: And who is Mitke?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He worked with my brother in the electrical industry plant. He was head of police or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR OLUJIC
utterances.text: Head of police where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Konjic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR OLUJIC
utterances.text: And where was he while you were in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He came to Celebici to visit people he knew. On one occasion he brought a sandwich for my brother.

utterances.speaker: MR OLUJIC
utterances.text: So he entered the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR OLUJIC
utterances.text: Did any other people come to the camp apart from him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The camp? The hangar? I don't know who came to the camp but to the hangar oh, yes, yes, there were people. Some young men from Mostar, some kind of Ustashas. I forgot to mention this. They didn't beat all of us, but some of us, and on one of their beatings my ulcer perforated. I had to go to the infirmary. So we were beaten by many foreign people, so to speak, people outside the camp and not just the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR OLUJIC
utterances.text: Did you do your military service in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR OLUJIC
utterances.text: Did you acquire a rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR OLUJIC
utterances.text: Did you go to the school of reserve non-commissioned officers as it was called then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR OLUJIC
utterances.text: In your statement you said that you had a rifle. Do you know how to put a rifle together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I could do it now.

utterances.speaker: MR OLUJIC
utterances.text: But you served in the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did know then. I don't know whether I could now.

utterances.speaker: MR OLUJIC
utterances.text: Do you know how to use a rifle to fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't. I've forgotten how to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr M, I have completed my set of questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr Moran?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it will take a second for us to get situated here. May it please the court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, my name is Tom Moran and I represent Hazim Delic here and I'm going to ask you some questions and I don't think it will take all that long, but I think we can shorten this a little bit if you'll do a couple of things for me. First, if you'll listen to the question and just answer the question. Some of them may just require a "yes" or "no". Could you do that for me, just answer exactly the question that I ask you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before you start asking your questions, I would beg the court's indulgence for a short break, if that is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you give him the break, I think I may be able to cut down the extent of my cross, if I have a chance to go over it and we may save us all a little bit of time and I have no objection to him having a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: We can give him a break and return about 4.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honours, and thank you on behalf of the witness also.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May it please the court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr Moran, you can go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Mr M, a couple of other things we talked about before the break and I just want to go over these. Sometimes I ask questions that are a little convoluted and a little hard to understand and sometimes they are confusing. If I ask you one of those questions, will you stop me, ask me to repeat it, rephrase it and do whatever I have to do so that you understand what I'm asking? I just notice that you nodded. The last thing I wanted to talk about was the nodding. There's two ladies in this courtroom, one sitting right up here and one over there who are what are called Court Reporters. Their job is to write down everything we say because everything we say has to be in the record. They couldn't write down a nod. So if you could answer the question, if it's a "yes" or a "no" instead of nodding yes or no, if you could say "yes" or "no", they can get it down into the record. Would you think about doing that? I know it's sometimes a little hard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now what I'm going to do so there's not going to be any surprises for you, I am going to go over your testimony and ask you a few questions maybe to clarify some of the things you already said. Basically I'm going to go in the same order that the Prosecutor went in her direct examination. There may be a few things where I'll jump around but I'll try to remember to tell you that before I do it so you're not going to be surprised; okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just get a couple of quick preliminary things out of the way. What kind of automatic rifle did you have, sir; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An automatic weapon made in Kragujevac.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, if I show you some pictures can you pick out the one that looks like the weapon you had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, if you just flip through those and see if you recognise one that's similar to the one that you had.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think this one looks most like the one I had.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Now there are some more pictures that the usher has. If you will set that one aside and flip through those and see if you see one that looks a little bit more like it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think this is the one.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. On the back, sir, there's some numbers. If you'll flip it over, it will be like "D/4/something" with a letter. Could you read those out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's in English.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe the usher can --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't speak English.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: I understand. I thought that you might be able to just read the letters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Could you put it on the ELMO, please, so that the members of the court could see it? The other side, the photo. Again that silver thing down at the bottom, did you have one of those? It looks like a bomb. You didn't have that, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Just the rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Judge Odio Benito, I think this is the same one we talked about in the past?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let us talk a little bit about after you surrendered. By the way, you did surrender the weapon that looked like that one to the Muslim authorities when you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: And did you have any ammunition for it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but only in the magazine. I don't know how many.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. So you just had one magazine? Is that all you had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the rifle and I don't know how many more bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Did you fire any of those bullets during the defence of Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Did you shoot at someone or did you just shoot up in the air?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I didn't see anyone. I didn't shoot at anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: So did you just shoot the bullets in the air? Is that what you did, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the air, just to let them know that we were there, so that the people couldn't just come in.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. Let me jump forward a little bit to after you were arrested. Remember you said you were brought to some vehicles before you were taken to Celebici and you were forced on to the vehicles. About 20 of you were the first group and another 30 were later brought in. Do you remember saying that on direct examination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Did those people abuse you or mistreat you in any way while you were being transported?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Could you elaborate on that? What kind of things did they do to you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When surrendering, a man went ahead with a white flag. Behind him there were about 20 of us. At a distance of 20 or 30 metres we were noticed and stopped. They said we could go forward, hand in our weapons and nothing would happen to us. That is what we did. We approached the butcher's shop, that is the centre of the village. We were lined up there, facing the butcher's shop. We had to take a step forward, to place the ammunition and weapons down. Then we had to go back to the line and we were placed on the white line in the middle of the road. The truck was about 50 metres away near the butcher's shop. We had to follow one another. They made a gauntlet on both sides and they beat us with butts, with kicks, up to the point when we reached the trucks, so that there was 50 metres that we had to cover and all that time we were beaten. Some of us fell down. We would lift each other. Upon climbing on the truck we were beaten again. It was very high. There were some elderly people. Some of them were already weak from the beating. They would fall. Again we would help each other. So upon climbing on to the truck we were beaten again. So that was during the loading on to the truck. Therefore, we had to pass through this gauntlet. We were beaten all the time up to the truck and while climbing on to the truck.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: And, in fact, you were beaten during the ride to Celebici, too, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not during the ride. We didn't know where we were going. We stopped two or three times. We were threatened that that was the place where we would be executed, dumped in the river, thrown over the slope. While we were being transported from the loading to Celebici we were not beaten, but we were threatened. Whenever they stopped, they threatened that they would kill us.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: In fact, sir, you testified on direct that when you were put into Tunnel 9 your left arm was seriously injured and it was bleeding. That injury was -- you got that injury while you were being loaded on to the trucks; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. The next question I want to ask you about is Ms McMurrey (sic) asked you about people taking your gold and watches and keys and things when you arrived at Celebici. Do you remember testifying about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: And you remained continuously in some kind of detention, either at Celebici or at Musala, or some place until, what, October of 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: And in how many different places were you confined?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first it was Tunnel Number 9. Then it was Hangar Number 6. Then it was Musala and in Musala I was moved five or six times to different cells.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: So you were in at least two completely separate detention facilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: And was any of that property returned to you when you were released, completely released from detention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: And you don't know what happened to that property between the time that you arrived at Celebici and the time that you were released some, what, two years later, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the property that I had on me or the property that I had at home?

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: The property you had on you. All you know is that it was taken away when you got to Celebici and nobody ever gave it back to you; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Who is Rale, R-A-L-E?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rale -- during the time when the prisoners were unloaded, when they were arriving in Celebici, I heard -- I personally heard Rale saying: "Don't beat them because I'm here. I wanted to use this because I could have been the third or the fifth coming up. I tried to get off there at the time. I got off. I saw Rale to the left of me as he was entering a car and then he left. So I made a mistake because he left and then I was there. Then I was beaten, but the first three fared the best.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Rale was -- do you have any idea what Rale's job was at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the second group was brought in, and this is the group where my father and brother were in, and after they were brought in Rale arrived close to the dawn and opened up Number 9, took several people out and somehow ironically said: "So what did they do to you?" I could hear the irony in his voice. So Rale was someone who was supposedly surprised by what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Did it appear to you that Rale had some position of authority in the camp at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it did, since he told the guards: "Don't beat them, because I'm here" while they were beating those three. I don't know if he had any authority over these people or over the whole camp, but he seemed to have had influence.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: He kind of looked like the Commander, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Now I'm going to jump ahead and ask you one real quick question about Tunnel 9 and then I'm going to change the subject again; okay? Maybe a couple of questions about Tunnel 9. Inside Tunnel 9 was there any kind of a bucket that was down, way down at the bottom, right by those solid doors at the bottom, for people to use in relieving themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I was very close to that place where the people relieved themselves and there was no container of any kind there.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: So if some other people remembered one, they were remembering it wrong or they were in Tunnel 9 at a different time from you, something like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe later, because I was there for just seven or eight days and then I was transferred to Number 6. So maybe later, but during my stay there there was nothing, there was no container, so people relieved themselves right there on the floor, on the concrete.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: That's fine. I'm going to jump ahead to another subject, and that's this: you testified on direct that at some point you were taken out and beaten, and the way that this occurred was you had to kneel down, put your hands behind your head and somebody gave you karate kicks on the chest; right? Remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: I'm just asking you if you remember testifying on direct examination that at some point you were taken out of Hangar 6 and you were told to kneel down and put your hands behind your head, and then someone started giving you karate kicks on the chest? Do you remember that incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. I also know who it was. It's not just someone, because I know who it was. I know it in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Well, I think you' already testified about that. I just wanted to clarify a couple of things. One, those karate kicks on the chest, were they right on your chest area? Do you know what the bone called the sternum is? It is the breast bone right down the middle of your chest. Was that where those kicks were, along in here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, from the throat down to the navel area. So this was the chest area but I only remember when I bent my head a little bit, I got a kick right here in the chin, but no, those kicks were aimed right at the chest.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: They were -- you were being kicked as hard as you could be kicked, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and there was a soldier's boot.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Yes. You were kicked, what, about 80 times; wasn't that about right? Somebody counted them out, 80 times, 80 kicks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody counted. There was no count. I just know that it was a large number. I think that I could have been able to count up to half of those and then after that I was unable to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: So it was at least 40. You would agree with me you were kicked at least 40 times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Many more.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: But at least?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But many more, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: And I think you said that there weren't any visible signs of injury from that beating; is that right? Isn't that what you said on direct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. No outside injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: So I could look at you or the judges could have looked at you, anybody could have looked at you, and they wouldn't have seen any injuries; that is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Except the red skin and some bruises, black and blue. So the skin was more bluish, black-bluish, but no lacerations, but nobody could see this because I was wearing a shirt.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let me jump to another area. You served some time in the JNA, about fifteen months?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Da.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Now as part of your training in the DNA, did you receive training in chemical warfare?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Did you ever use a gas mask while you were in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very infrequently.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: It is the same in my army because they are just horrible to have to put on and have to wear those things. I'm going to ask you about the one that you said was put on your face in Celebici. I'm going to ask you to describe it a little bit. Let me see if I can -- as I understand it, what it is, it's a thing that covers your face and it's got a very tight seal along the side of your face; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's a military gas mask that covers the face, the front part of the head and then is tightened up from behind.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: It's like the one you used when you were in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: And it's got filters that would clean the air so you could breathe in; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: And then there's a valve that can close the air off; is that true? It closes off the filters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: When the filters are closed -- when the filter is open, you can breathe fairly normally; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: And when the filters are closed you can't breathe any air in at all; isn't that right -- not the filter -- the valve is closed, you cannot breathe anything in at all; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you cannot breathe at all. There's a little black lid that is put on top of the filter so the air cannot come in.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: How long were you in this filter -- in this mask with the filters covered like that during this beating? Ten minutes, fifteen minutes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how long, but the entire time I was trying to lift it. Sometimes I would be able to pull the mask off a little bit so that I could get some air, not directly, but through the side. So occasionally I would get a little bit of air, but through the beating the mask was on, and that could have been going on for 10, 15, 20 minutes. It appears as a very long period of time when you're being beaten. To me it looked like an eternity.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: A couple of other questions and then I'm going to, I think, be done. Actually two other areas. Let me get one real quick. You testified on cross-examination I believe from Mr Olujic, but don't hold me to that, that you got a perforated ulcer at some point in the camp; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Did you receive any medical treatment for that? Did you have surgery or anything to stop the bleeding from the perforated ulcer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I could even explain, if I may. I would wish to explain it.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My ulcer perforated. I think it was from the blows of one of the people who were not the guards. Those were the persons -- they called themselves Ustasha from Listice. One strong, well-built guy hit me with his -- he held a pistol in his hand. So he hit me in the stomach with that and I lost my breath and I felt -- I passed out and then I had bleeding and I asked for help. My brother then asked for somebody, a guard, and he said that he would ask Delic and Delic came. He took me -- in fact, my brother and another prisoner took me. They carried me over to the infirmary, and Delic was in the car, so he was driving behind them. So they had to hurry up, because he was coming up behind them in the car. I was examined by Dr Relja Mrkajic. He only asked Delic and these are the words -- he said: "Will he survive?", Delic said. Dr Mrkajic said: "Yes". Then after that I spent the night and then I was told to pick up my stuff and go back. So those when I returned and so this was the one time that I received some medicine and that was the only time.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Now I promised you there was only going to be one area, but I am afraid you have opened up two more with that answer, but we'll still keep it real short for you; okay? You said that the people who beat you on that occasion were not in the camp. They weren't guards there. Does that mean that it was common or uncommon or what for people that were not part of the staff of Celebici to somehow gain entrance to the camp and abuse the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they could do that?

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: How often did that occur, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first it was much more frequent than later on. In other words, at first people who were not guards at all would come in and then later they were prevented from doing this, especially after the arrival of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: So basically as things got better organised in the camp, they became better able to keep out these intruders who were abusing the inmates, the detainees; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, but it is also true that the role of these people was then taken over by the guards, the people who were guarding us.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: You mentioned while you were in the infirmary Dr Mrkajic gave you some medicine. Was it just a painkiller or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. I know that I felt relief and that I had that twice and then after that again we had poor food and there was no medicine. So I felt very bad. In other words, I was not given proper treatment. I was not allowed to stay there and I had to go back to Number 6. In the infirmary the food was better and the care was better.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: And it was Hazim Delic that arranged for you to go to the infirmary on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He also organised for me to go back.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. This I think will be the last area we're going to talk about. I'm just tell you right up front why I'm going to go into it. You answered somebody on -- I think it was Ms Residovic -- on cross and it's about the reserve police; okay? Just your status with the reserve police. I just want to make sure I understand it. Let me tell you what I think your testimony was and if I'm wrong, tell me I'm wrong. Will you do that for me? Okay. As I understand it, there was a reserve police unit that was in Bradina that came under the jurisdiction of the Police Department, the MUP, in Konjic, and at some time in the Spring of 1992 all of the Croatian and Muslim members of that reserve police unit left the unit and at that point you were asked to join the reserve police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: And as reserve policemen, you did what policemen do. You were a police officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: And that's when you got your weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: And the uniform you were wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: By the way, I understand that you -- all the time you were in Celebici you wore the same clothes, the clothes you were arrested in; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Celebici, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: And that was your police uniform; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I was not arrested in my police uniform. I was arrested in my civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: So you had an automatic weapon when you surrendered but you were not wearing a uniform; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would pass the witness. The only other thing I have is I just want to get on the record the number of that picture on the stand. When it is brought back to the Registrar, if he would just read that into the record. There is apparently some confusion over exactly what the Exhibit Number is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could get that Exhibit Number read?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: What is the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit that was identified by the witness is D15/H.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: May I proceed now, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr Ackerman, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr M, may name is John Ackerman. I represent Mr Landzo. Good afternoon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going to try to ask you questions that are easily understood and if you don't understand a question that I ask you, could you please let me know that you don't understand it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to know, first of all, how many times you have talked to other people before arriving at this court about your experiences at Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Could you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. How many times have you talked to people about your experiences at Celebici camp before today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How many times? It's difficult to say how many times. Of course I spoke about my experiences with my mother and my father, my relatives and friends. I don't know how many times.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How many times have you talked about those experiences with people in some kind of authority, prosecutors, people who work for prosecutors, organisations, things of that nature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm afraid it's unclear to me your question. I spoke to people who are in Belgrade, in the detainees association. I personally am writing memoires on my experiences in the camp. I don't know who you are referring to, which officials. Whom do you have in mind exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me see if I can get more specific and I think maybe the Registrar has anticipated where we're going next. I want to show you some photographs and tell me if you can recognise any of the people depicted in these photographs. I think there are three; correct? What I'd like you to do is once you look at them, then put them over there on that ELMO so we can all see the ones you are referring to. Could you do that, please? The arms on that ELMO need to be extended a little bit so that light doesn't shine right straight down on the -- yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr Bjelica is the only one I recognise, no-one else.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. That's a person -- you just got a close-up of his chest. You recognise that person and you know that person; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The other two photographs that you were shown are people that you've not seen before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I have never seen them before.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, first of all, with regard to the person whom you indicate that you do know, have you discussed your experiences at Celebici camp with that person, Dr Bjelica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dr Bjelica, upon my release from the camp, enabled a detailed check-up, medical check-up, and he made it possible for me to get the appropriate medicine, and he helped me a lot. He X-rayed my ribs, my chest and my pelvis. So he was the man who examined me, gave me the medicines I needed and helped me.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have the X-rays he took of your chest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in Belgrade. I think he has them.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Didn't he give them to you for you to take home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he didn't give them to me, because I was supposed to come again for an examination. In the meantime I had to leave, I had to travel, so that I didn't go back there.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were there any blood tests or any other tests beyond the X-rays that were done while you visited Dr Bjelica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He carried out a complete test of my blood, my urine, all X-rays of my lungs, a detailed medical examination.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And before you left there did he give you all of the results of all of the tests to take with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I just said no, because I had intended to go back to see him again.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Petar Fiodorev?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: To your knowledge you have never spoken with that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Branko Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know a person who claims to be the coordinator of the Association for the Tribunal in The Hague? Do you know who that might be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How long has it been since you had occasion to visit the offices of the Association of Detainees in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean after my release from prison?

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No. I'm talking about today. How long has it been since you have been there? Were you there last week?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Roughly maybe two years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you a member of the Association?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Association of what?

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The Association of Detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were you ever a member of the Association of Detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I just visited the Association. Immediately after my release I went to the premises of the Association, but I was never a member.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I take it you visited the Association for the purpose of giving them a statement regarding your experiences at Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And do you know where that statement is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know where the statement is. I don't know that -- I do know that I didn't make such a statement. I just said how long I had spent in prison, when I entered, when I was released. I didn't give a complete statement, because, as I said, I'm writing my memoires. So I kept it to myself. So I didn't make a statement about all that happened in Celebici, about my whole stay in Celebici, just certain general facts, when admitted, when released, who was there. So a very short statement, maybe one typed page, not more.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I take it you've not seen that since that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have it with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When did you last see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe seven or eight months ago.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Where was it when you saw it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the place?

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Where did you see the statement? Who had it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't tell you and I don't want to tell you where I was, but I found the statement in a written document, in a book which is a collection. So I saw my statement printed in a document.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell me what that document is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is it a printed book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said I wouldn't like to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask that he be ordered to answer that question. I think it's an important question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I don't know how important it is to you. He says he will not answer it. If there's anything that might incriminate him, he might not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He has not said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: If he is unwilling, then there must be some fears.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is an awfully important issue, because we have been enquiring now for weeks about what has happened to the statements that we understand were given to the Association of Detainees. The Prosecutor's office has represented they don't have them and has never seen them. It all of a sudden appears that this witness knows where they are, that they are published in a book and I think they might be extremely valuable for purposes of impeachment in cross-examination of witnesses. So I think we are entitled to know what this book is and how we might be able to get our hands on it. If he is concerned about saying this in public session, I would be delighted to go into private session so he can say it that way. If he is not willing to say it even in private session, I would be happy for him to write it down so we can get it that way. I think we are entitled to this information. If this witness has made a prior statement that may be useful for impeaching him and has disclosed to us the location of other statements that might exist from other witnesses, then I think we are entitled to that information. If the Prosecutor knows what he is talking about, they ought to disclose it to us as part of their obligation to provide us with information that they know about. So as a final last ditch effort I think the Prosecutor could be instructed to ask him in private and give us that information, but I think we're absolutely entitled to it, until such time as this witness might say that revealing this information might have some tendency to incriminate him, and then, of course, he would be protected by the rules, but he has not gotten to that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, he has refused. If you have any other means of exploring how to get it from him, you might do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: On behalf of the prosecution, we certainly -- we are willing to talk to the witness privately to find out what kind of concerns he has. They may well be concerns about disclosing where he lives or other people. So if it's necessary -- I'm not sure that I believe it's necessary -- but the Prosecution would certainly be willing to do that privately.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Please understand that I have no interest whatsoever in where you live, Mr M, and I'm not asking you that. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have understood that. This document is the personal archives of a friend of mine. I saw this personally. Many people haven't seen it and I absolutely do not wish to disclose it. You asked me where I saw it and when, so you want to know where I live, how I live, who are my friends, which company I mix with, and that is something I don't want to disclose.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will not ask you any of those questions that you just mentioned but I will ask you to tell us the name of the person who has this statement and other statements that are published in a book.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot tell you. It is a friend. It is his personal documentation and it has nothing to do with this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, this witness has come here and given direct testimony in this case. He is now subject to cross-examination. I think it's an absolute denial for the right of cross-examination for this witness to be able to choose which questions he will answer and which ones he won't. I, therefore, move that his entire testimony before this Tribunal be stricken or in the alternative that he be ordered to answer the questions asked of him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You might as well give your reply to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would strongly object. It is very often the case that witnesses may know -- may not want to for safety considerations or any other considerations not want to give the identity of certain persons and, in fact, I believe there's a provision in the rules which indicates that persons can have confidential information. I would also state that to the extent that there may well be circumstances where your Honours would want to direct someone to answer something, this is not one of them. The idea that some years ago this witness may have given a less than one page statement, which only contained when he went to Celebici and when he was released, certainly cannot be considered the kind of important information that deprives the accused of cross-examination. We think this is far and beyond, and the witness is entitled, I believe, to keep confidential such information that he -- where he doesn't know the desires of the person who may have this, and the idea that this would be necessary for this kind of thing, so that the defence can find this potentially -- can find this very short statement I do not believe is necessary for cross-examination. It may well be that many people, many witnesses often have given statements to government agencies, NGOs, you know, the defence, but there's no requirement anywhere, nor is it part of common sense, that the defence must be entitled to explore every single statement before effectively cross-examining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But wouldn't that be the first statement which the witness made after his release from Celebici and wouldn't it be on that account very relevant?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has already said with respect to this statement that it is a very brief statement that did not discuss his experiences but just discussed general information, such as when he went to Celebici and when he got out of Celebici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But he knows where that statement is. It is in a friend's archives.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He knows where that statement is because it is in his friend's archives. Can't you obtain a copy of that statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Certainly the Prosecution has indicated that it is happy to talk to this witness privately to determine more about this, but given what this witness has said, which is that it is a very brief statement, and I don't believe that there's any need for it, but the Prosecution is certainly willing to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the record of this witness' testimony goes beyond the representation of Ms McHenry. He said that the statement was probably only a page long, but it wasn't just when he got into Celebici and when he got out. He said that it talked about who was there. Now who was there could be awfully important to what we're doing here. The larger issue really tends to put us all on the horns of a very large dilemma. We have been suggesting now for some time and have provided evidence to this Chamber that each of these detainees gave statements to the Association of Detainees in Belgrade at some point. The Prosecution has denied any knowledge of that. They have told us they have made efforts to acquire those statements. They have told us that there are no such statements. We have asked other witnesses that have come here from the Association of Detainees that have been there, who said: "No. No statements, no statements". That's what we've gotten over and over and over. Now all of a sudden a witness comes and says that he has seen a book, a personal compilation of apparently statements that detainees made at the Association of Detainees. Now it may be that this person's statement is one page long. It's hard to say what's contained in that one page but there are likely statements in there from other detainees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Unless we can get to the bottom of that, we are really in a fairly large dilemma. Second of all, Rule 77 of the Tribunal says that: "A witness who refuses or fails to answer a question relevant to the issue before the Chamber may be found in contempt of the Tribunal". I'm not going so far as to ask the court to find this gentleman in contempt, but simply to order him to answer the question or strike his testimony, one or the other. If he's not willing to be subject to cross-examination, then his direct testimony should not be a part of your consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think in certain cases when a witness is unable to submit -- give an answer which might to a large extent satisfy the defence, he might say so clearly. I think he said he knows where it is. At the most if we follow the undertaking of the Prosecution, it might give us the name and possibly how to get at this friend who has this statement. Perhaps that might be possible. I do not think he can be compelled to disclose the name of the friend in open session anyway. I wouldn't want him to. Whichever way you put it, these proceedings have been a very delicate one in several cases. Not only so many things might have been happening and if somebody is legitimately suspicious of certain things about the evidence he might give, one should have some respect for that view.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I agree with what you have just said. I certainly do not want to take any steps here that would put any individual in any kind of personal danger. Therefore, I temper the remarks that I make with that. However, anything that we can do that would help this Chamber to find the truth, then I think it's important that we take that step in an attempt to find the truth. As Judge Jan has pointed out, if this statement and other statements are the first statements that these people made after leaving Celebici, they might be the most important and most revealing statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Frankly I don't want to be insensitive to the interests of the accused persons. I know everything is concerning the trial as a whole. Sometimes if you push perhaps certain privileges too far, it might open the hornets' nest which otherwise no-one wants to. I agree we might persuade the Prosecution to go some way to try to find that out, these statements, but I do not think it is correct merely because he has indicated this statement exists somewhere, he has to be pushed to the limits of it. We will do everything to get that. I think Ms McHenry has given, I wouldn't say an undertaking, but perhaps she might make some efforts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
