utterances.text: I think where we are, the Prosecutor is going to look into this matter in some detail with the witness and hopefully have some kind of an answer for us in the morning. I am wondering if it might not be appropriate to go ahead and recess now for the evening and see what that answer is in the morning before I pursue this line any further, or if you would like me to go on to another matter, I can do that too. It is up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You can go on to another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. You have told us that you are in the process of writing your memoires of your experiences, I take it during the war. Is that fairly complete in manuscript form at this point or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a manuscript.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And have you provided a copy of that to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. I'm not going to give the Prosecutor my memoires.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you bring a copy of it with you when you came here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you intend for this simply to be your private memoires or do you hope to have it published?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have had offers from publishing houses, but I want this to be my personal affair. For the present I do not wish to publish it. Maybe at some later stage, but for the present, no. I want to keep it for myself. I may even print it for my own benefit, but at present it's in manuscript form.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So I take it you've kept it totally to yourself and not shared it with other persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only my closest friends, but not the public.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you use that manuscript in any respect to help you prepare yourself to give your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What is it that you looked at to help you refresh your memory for your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing at all. My memory is sufficiently fresh. These are things one does not forget.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you have any conversation with Ms McHenry regarding what your testimony would be here today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With Ms McHenry I spoke about these things, about the method of work, on the position of witnesses, on translation, about my protection, that I wanted to be protected. I received assurances that I would not be seen, that I would not be taped -- shown to the public. She explained to me how the interpretation works, how the Tribunal works. She answered my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You didn't go over the testimony you were going to give here at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Even she doesn't know what people will ask me. We spoke about general things in preparation of this testimony. The method of work, that I should wait for the interpretation, and that kind of thing. She read to me my statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Just to clarify, I think when defence counsel ask if they -- if you went over the testimony, I think to some witnesses that may mean did you practise? Were you told the questions that would be asked? I think if defence counsel would ask was anything about what happened at Celebici discussed or did she ask you any questions, you might get a different answer to the question of "you didn't go over the testimony".

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I guess now that you have heard that, you can tell me that you, in fact, discussed your experiences at Celebici with Ms McHenry prior to giving your testimony here, can you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What you just told us was that you had an opportunity to either read your statement to the OTP or have that statement read to you by Ms McHenry; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what you've also told us was that it was really totally unnecessary to have that statement read to you or to consult any other statement that you might have made, because you have such a crisp and clear memory of everything that happened to you at Celebici. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was quite sufficient for me to read my statement. I do remember things, but sometimes one gets a little confused. It is my statement that I wanted to re-read.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to take a copy of it with you out of this building to your hotel, so that you could spend some time studying it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And would it have been -- would it have been yesterday that you had an opportunity to see it or hear it read to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would it have been Friday, Saturday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thursday -- I think it was Friday or Saturday -- no, I think it was Saturday.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So two or three days ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you only had to remember what was in your statement for two or three days to be able to completely reflect in your testimony here today what you had said in your statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I think not. I don't know how you understand this, but I know that the statement I made was correct and that I personally asked for this statement to be read to me. Nobody forced me, nor told me to say this, so that I claim that my statement is correct. I remember what I said there. I have the feeling that you are under the impression that somebody persuaded me what to say. No. What is said in that statement is the truth. It's not something that was made up.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I really didn't understand that to be the force of any of my questions. My questions have to do with when was the last time you reviewed your statement before you came in here to testify today and I think you've told me that was Saturday; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I said clearly it was Saturday.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you've not had an opportunity since Saturday to see it again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And do you think between Saturday and today you have forgotten anything that was in your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the questions are rather provocative. I can never forget what happened to me.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Cross-examination is supposed to be provocative. That's what it's designed to be. It's to test your truth-telling and those kinds of things. Now the question that I asked you was: have you forgotten, since Saturday, the things that you read that were in your statement? That is the question I want to know?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Objection. Asked and answered. The witness has already indicated that he remembers what happened and that his statement was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Actually, your Honours, he hasn't answered that. I can see it right on the screen. His answer had nothing to do with my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That is from Saturday to Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Those are the days.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: But his earlier answers have been he will never forget what has happened to him. That refers to this period. That was the statement he made to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Except you think my interpretation is wrong, but this is exactly what he has just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If that's what the court believes he said, I'll accept that and go on to the next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. Go on to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If I just may again ask for clarification, I think when the witness was asked about who read his statement over and if it was -- I don't think it is clear that the statement was read over to him in full. I might with all due respect ask that defence counsel might want to ask whether or not the entire statement was read to him and, if so, by whom, because I think there may be some confusion about that also.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Ms McHenry wants me to ask you if anyone read your whole statement to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I think it was the whole statement that was read to me.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Who was it that read it to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did personally.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you read it yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you read a Serbo-Croatian version of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I thought you had told us earlier that someone had read it to you. Was that a -- did I misunderstand you about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I personally read it in the Serbo-Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Was there ever a time when Ms McHenry read part of it to you to remind you of parts of it or anything? Do you recall her reading any of it to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I think not. The statement was there. I read it. If there may have been a printing error, I could correct it and that was all. There were no errors in the statement, nor any technical errors of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. The statement which you read on Saturday, having already a crystal clear memory of your experiences, when you testified here this morning, you recall, of course, being asked about the brothers Dordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you recall being asked about a sexual incident that went on with the brothers Dordic? You recall that, do you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It is true, isn't it, that in your review of your statement it was very clear in your statement that you had named a couple of the guards having been involved in that; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall. I don't remember the names of the guards, just now anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it's true that in your testimony this morning you also said that you didn't remember the names of the guards that you had said in your statement might have been involved in that incident. That's what you said this morning in your testimony too; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I can't remember their names. Maybe when I made the statement I still remembered, because that was earlier on, but I just don't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But you re-read that statement as short a time ago as Saturday and you've forgotten again since Saturday with this crystal clear memory you talk about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I've forgotten the names of the guards. I didn't read it so carefully. I didn't pay so much attention. I simply forgot the names of the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, did you understand that what you were coming to do here is a pretty serious matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Don't you think it's important to be careful in the process of preparing yourself and giving your testimony here?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. I think this is not a fair question for examination. There's nothing about what this witness has said that indicates that he is doing anything other than testifying truthfully about his memory. I think this is improper.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, he just said he didn't read his statement carefully. I was just exploring that statement that he made, that he wasn't being careful on Saturday when he read his statement. So I think it was absolutely invited by his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. His statement is already made. Whether he read it carefully or not, I think it's a statement. It depends on what use one makes of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, I have a great deal more. This little tiny piece of what I was going to ask him stretched into this amount of time. I think I am going to be at least another hour. Would you like me to proceed now or would you like to break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: No. We will break and we'll come back tomorrow morning at 10 o'clock, but before we break, Ms McHenry, it might be helpful to persuade the witness that all that is required is the statement and not whatever he is concerned about, because of the statement he made to someone about a particular issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I will certainly explore the issue and report to your Honours and defence counsel tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Because definitely whoever is his friend who might have got the statement into his book, he cannot be responsible for that statement. Whether he is not in a position to get that statement if it is used for impeachment purposes. This is what counsel is suggesting. If there's anything in it which can affect his testimony before the Trial Chamber. I suppose that is what you want him to produce.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Thank you very much. I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: So the Trial Chamber will now rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: --ooOoo--
